NJ Foreclosure & Injury Guide
30/60/90 planAbout

For injured New Jersey drivers and passengers

Hurt in a New Jersey car accident and behind on your mortgage?

The short answer: your injury claim and your foreclosure run on two different clocks, and the mortgage clock is usually faster. A servicer generally cannot file the first foreclosure paper until you are more than 120 days behind, and New Jersey then gives you a written notice, a right to cure up to final judgment and a free court mediation program. Meanwhile your own PIP policy and NJ Temporary Disability Insurance can replace part of your pay right now, long before any settlement. Use those benefits, call the servicer early and treat the injury settlement as the last money in, not the first.

$100 a weekstandard PIP income continuation, capped at $5,200, unless you bought more

Which moves faster, the injury claim or the foreclosure?

The foreclosure, almost always. A New Jersey injury claim cannot settle well until your doctors know how badly you are hurt, and a claim that ends up in court can take years. Our main site's guide on how long NJ car accident settlements take counted 11 New Jersey crash injury lawsuits that went to the Appellate Division: the median was 4 calendar years from filing to the appeal decision. Most claims settle faster than that, but none of them settle in the 120 days a mortgage servicer has to wait.

The people we hear from also start late. In anonymised intake data known to the publisher (547 New Jersey injury calls from 2023 to 2026 with a usable crash date), the median caller first phoned a law firm 156 days after the crash. Only 25% called within 30 days, and 18% waited more than two years. If you stopped paying the mortgage when your paycheck stopped, day 156 is already past the 120-day line in the federal rule. And the most common reason the firm turned a caller down was that the two-year filing deadline had already passed.

The practical lesson: the money that can save the house in the first six months is benefit money (PIP income continuation, Temporary Disability, any employer short-term disability) plus whatever relief the servicer agrees to. Settlement money usually arrives later.

What does PIP pay for lost income in New Jersey?

On a Standard Policy, PIP includes income continuation: payment of your lost income if your crash injuries keep you from working, whoever caused the crash. The statute sets the base benefit at a maximum of $100 a week, with a total limit of $5,200 per person per accident, and it can never exceed the net income you normally earned for that period (N.J.S.A. 39:6A-4(b)). That is 52 weeks at the full $100.

Income-related PIP options on a New Jersey auto policy
Your policyIncome continuationWhere the rule comes from
Standard Policy, Extra PIP Package keptUp to $100 a week, $5,200 total, net of normal incomeN.J.S.A. 39:6A-4(b)
Standard Policy, Extra PIP Package declinedNone. You can opt out of income continuation, essential services, death and funeral benefits as a packageN.J.S.A. 39:6A-4.3(b); DOBI Buyer's Guide
Standard Policy, extra amounts boughtMore than the base, only for loss above $100 a week / $5,200, at the level you choseN.J.S.A. 39:6A-10 (insurers must make extra cover available)
Basic PolicyMedical expense PIP only ($15,000, up to $250,000 for certain injuries); the Extra PIP Package is a Standard Policy optionDOBI Buyer's Guide

DOBI's 2026 Buyer's Guide says most consumers keep the Extra PIP Package. Do not assume you did: look at the declarations page or Coverage Selection Form in force on the crash date. If more than one auto policy could apply (for example you were a passenger), ask the adjuster in writing which policy is paying.

How to claim it: PIP is paid "as loss accrues, upon written notice" (N.J.S.A. 39:6A-6). In practice that means you send the PIP adjuster a wage verification from your employer (or tax returns if you are self-employed) and a doctor's disability note covering the dates you were out. A PIP payment is overdue if not paid within 60 days after the insurer gets written notice of the loss and its amount, and overdue payments carry interest (N.J.S.A. 39:6A-5(g), (h)). One useful protection for a stretched household: PIP benefits cannot be assigned (except to medical providers) and are not subject to levy, execution or attachment for debts (N.J.S.A. 39:6A-4). A creditor cannot garnish your PIP wage checks.

For medical limits, deductibles and the 20% co-pay, see our main site's breakdown of what NJ PIP covers and where the limits sit.

How does NJ Temporary Disability Insurance interact with PIP?

NJ Temporary Disability Insurance (TDI) pays when an off-the-job condition, including a car crash injury, stops you working. The state Department of Labor says it pays 85% of your average weekly wage, up to a 2026 maximum of $1,119 a week, for up to 26 weeks. To qualify in 2026 you need 20 base weeks earning at least $310 a week, or $15,500 in the base year. You can apply from your first day of disability and have 30 days after your leave starts to file, and there is an unpaid waiting week built into the law.

The two benefits do not stack. New Jersey law says TDI collectible by you is deducted from PIP income continuation (N.J.S.A. 39:6A-6), and DOBI describes income continuation as paying "lost wages, less Temporary Disability Benefits you may receive." If you are entitled to TDI and do not apply, the PIP insurer can go to the TDI payer for reimbursement of what it paid. So the order is:

  1. Apply for TDI first (or your employer's private plan) within 30 days. It is usually the bigger check.
  2. Claim PIP income continuation for the gap between TDI and your lost wages, up to your weekly limit. On a base $100 a week policy, the gap PIP fills is small while TDI pays.
  3. Plan for week 27. TDI stops at 26 weeks. If you are still out, PIP income continuation may then be your only wage benefit, and your remaining $5,200 (or higher bought limit) matters a lot more.

Ask the PIP adjuster to put the offset math in writing. How the TDI deduction is applied against your weekly cap depends on your policy wording, and a written calculation is far easier to challenge than a phone call.

What if PIP stopped paying after an insurer medical exam?

This is the pattern we see most in the survivor support group we work with. Of 36 coded posts from a 4.6K-member car-accident survivors group (shared with members' consent), 16 described legal or insurance problems, and 5 described an insurer cutting off or denying care.

J., New Jersey

J. was hit head-on by a drunk driver in 2024. The injuries included whiplash and occipital neuralgia, the nerve pain that runs from the base of the skull. After the PIP insurer sent J. to its own medical exam, PIP stopped paying for treatment, and J. has been covering the care out of pocket since, about a year and a half after the crash. Paraphrased with permission; details limited to protect privacy.

New Jersey's PIP rules give you specific rights around that exam (N.J.A.C. 11:3-4.7(e)):

  • The exam must be scheduled within 7 calendar days of the notice, unless you agree to more time.
  • It must be done by a provider in the same discipline as your treating provider (a chiropractor for chiropractic care, for example), at a location reasonably convenient to you.
  • The insurer must tell you and your doctor whether it will keep paying no later than 3 business days after the exam.
  • If the examiner writes a report, you are entitled to a copy on request. Ask for it in writing the same week.

The appeal route. Your treating provider, if you assigned benefits to them, must first use the insurer's internal appeal (N.J.A.C. 11:3-4.7B). After that, or directly as the injured person, a PIP dispute can go to binding dispute resolution administered for the state by Forthright (N.J.S.A. 39:6A-5.1; N.J.A.C. 11:3-5.6). When the fight is about medical necessity or whether the injury is crash-related, the dispute resolution professional can send it to a medical review organization, whose finding is presumed correct but can be rebutted. If the award says the care was necessary, it is paid with interest.

For the mortgage, this matters twice. First, every out-of-pocket medical bill is money not going to the servicer. Second, the IME report often becomes the insurer's evidence that you can work, which can also affect income continuation. Keep every receipt and every denial letter: unpaid medical costs above your PIP coverage are part of what you can claim from the at-fault driver.

Can you claim the rest of your lost wages from the at-fault driver?

Yes. The lawsuit option you picked limits only pain and suffering claims. DOBI's Buyer's Guide says choosing the limitation on lawsuit option "does not affect your ability to sue for economic damages such as medical expenses and lost wages." What you cannot do is collect the same dollars twice: amounts paid or collectible under your PIP are kept out of the case against the other driver (N.J.S.A. 39:6A-12). The same section keeps your right to recover "uncompensated economic loss," including unreimbursed medical expenses above your PIP limits.

So the at-fault driver's claim is where you recover wage loss above $100 a week (or above your bought limit), wage loss after PIP runs out, and wage loss you never had PIP for. Our main site walks through claiming lost wages after a New Jersey car accident, including how your share of fault cuts the amount. Two practical points for homeowners:

  • Document lost income monthly, not at the end. Pay stubs before and after, employer letters, and a running total make it easy to show the wage loss and easy to show the servicer your hardship.
  • Watch the two-year clock. An injury lawsuit in New Jersey generally has to be filed within two years. Our NJ claim deadline calculator gives you the date in a few seconds.

How does a New Jersey residential foreclosure actually move?

New Jersey forecloses through the courts, and the Fair Foreclosure Act puts several fixed steps in front of a lender. Here they are in order, with the rule behind each.

Main steps in a NJ residential foreclosure
StepWhat happensYour deadline or right
1. Missed paymentsFederal servicing rules bar the first foreclosure notice or filing until the loan is more than 120 days delinquent (with narrow exceptions).Use this window to apply for loss mitigation (12 CFR 1024.41(f)).
2. Notice of Intention to ForecloseSent by registered or certified mail at least 30 days, and not more than 180 days, before the lender files. It must state the default, the exact cure amount, a cure date at least 30 days out, your mediation option and free housing counseling.Cure by the date in the notice to stop the filing (N.J.S.A. 2A:50-56). If more than 180 days pass, a new notice is required.
3. Complaint and summonsThe foreclosure case is filed in Superior Court and served on you, with notice of the mediation program.Answer within 35 days of service (R. 4:6-1). Ask for mediation within 60 days (R. 4:64-1B).
4. Right to cure continuesYou can still cure, de-accelerate and reinstate the loan by paying the arrears, late charges and capped court costs and fees.Any time up to final judgment; usable once every 18 months (N.J.S.A. 2A:50-57). A cure after filing leads to dismissal.
5. Final judgment and writIf the case is not resolved, the court enters final judgment and the sheriff is ordered to sell.Mediation can still be requested by motion at any time before the sale (R. 4:64-1B(c)(2)).
6. Sheriff saleNotice of sale is served by certified mail at least 10 days before the sale date (R. 4:65-2).The debtor can get two adjournments of up to 30 days each; the lender two; one more by agreement (N.J.S.A. 2A:17-36).
7. After the saleThe sheriff delivers the deed unless an objection is filed.A motion objecting to the sale must be served within 10 days after the sale (R. 4:65-5).

Notice what is missing from that table: any step where the court asks whether you have an injury claim coming. A pending settlement is not a defence to foreclosure. It can, however, be part of a realistic plan you show the servicer or a mediator, especially once you know roughly what it will net.

What is the NJ Foreclosure Mediation Program, and should you use it?

The Foreclosure Mediation Program is run by the New Jersey Judiciary, not by this website or any private company. It brings you and the lender together with a neutral mediator to look for a solution such as a loan modification, repayment plan or reinstatement, or, if keeping the house is not realistic, a deed in lieu of foreclosure, cash for keys, short sale or market sale (R. 4:64-1B(a)). The official information and forms are on the NJ Courts foreclosure self-help page.

Foreclosure Mediation Program at a glance
QuestionAnswer
Who qualifies?A homeowner in an active residential foreclosure case, where the property is your primary residence and a one to four family home, all borrowers on the note agree to take part, and you are not currently in bankruptcy (R. 4:64-1B(d)).
How do you ask?File a Mediation Request Statement with the Superior Court Clerk's Office, Foreclosure Mediation, P.O. Box 971, 25 Market Street, Trenton, NJ 08625, within 60 days of being served. After 60 days, by motion, any time before the sale.
What does it cost?Nothing. The homeowner is not required to pay any fees to take part (N.J.S.A. 2A:50-77(c)).
Is a counselor required?Yes. A trained foreclosure prevention counselor must sign a certification that you are cooperating with them before you can mediate (N.J.S.A. 2A:50-77(b)). The counseling is free through the program.
What happens next?Eligible homeowners get a Letter of Mediation Acceptance, and an initial conference is set within 45 days of it. Before that, the lender must mail you an itemized loan history and the amount needed to reinstate.
Does it stop the foreclosure?No. Unless the court orders otherwise, mediation does not stay the case. Keep meeting every court deadline (R. 4:64-1B(g)).
Does the lender have to cooperate?Both sides must negotiate in good faith, and the court can sanction a party that does not, including tolling interest, fees and costs.

Is it right for an injured homeowner? It is one option, and a good one when your income has dropped for a reason that is temporary and documented, because that is the story a modification or repayment plan is built around. It is less useful if you cannot show any income at all yet. That is another reason to get TDI and PIP income continuation flowing first. For counseling before any case is filed, NJ 2-1-1 lists the state's free foreclosure counseling and assistance options. Be wary of anyone who charges upfront to "save your home": the court program and its counseling cost nothing.

What should you ask your mortgage servicer for?

Call early, then put everything in writing. The servicer is the company on your monthly statement. Ask about:

  • Forbearance: a temporary pause or reduction of payments while you are medically unable to work. Ask how the missed amount gets repaid at the end, because a lump sum due in month 7 can recreate the problem.
  • Repayment plan: the arrears spread over several months on top of your normal payment, once income returns.
  • Loan modification: a permanent change to the rate, term or balance, usually based on your income after the injury.

Federal rules give a complete application real weight. The servicer must acknowledge your loss mitigation application in writing within 5 business days and tell you what is missing. If a complete application arrives more than 37 days before a foreclosure sale, the servicer must evaluate you for every option it offers within 30 days. If it arrives after the case is filed but still more than 37 days before the sale, the servicer cannot move for judgment or hold the sale while the application is pending (12 CFR 1024.41(b), (c), (g)). Small servicers have lighter duties under this rule but are still bound by the 120-day rule. The packet that works best for an injured borrower: a short hardship letter (crash date, injury, expected time out of work), your doctor's disability note, TDI and PIP award letters, and recent pay stubs or bank statements.

Do not tell the servicer your settlement "will cover everything" unless you know the net figure. Promises built on a gross number that later shrinks after fees and liens are how repayment plans fail.

A practical 30/60/90-day plan

What to do, counting from the crash
WhenIncome and injury claimMortgage
Days 1 to 30Open the PIP claim and send wage proof and a disability note. File for NJ TDI (30-day filing window). Find your declarations page: Extra PIP Package, limits, UM/UIM. Start a folder of receipts, denial letters and pay stubs.Call the servicer before you miss a payment if you can. Ask what forbearance or other hardship options exist and get the answer in writing. Keep paying anything you can.
Days 31 to 60Chase any PIP payment not made within 60 days of your written proof (it becomes overdue and carries interest). Speak to an injury lawyer about the at-fault claim and lost wages; ask whether the first review is free.Send a complete loss mitigation application. Note the 5-business-day acknowledgment and supply missing documents fast. If you have a notice of intention, read the cure amount and cure date.
Days 61 to 90If an insurer exam is scheduled, check the 7-day and same-discipline rules and request the report. If PIP cuts treatment, have your provider file the internal appeal and consider PIP dispute resolution.Contact a free foreclosure prevention counselor now, before day 120. If a complaint is served later, the 35-day answer and 60-day mediation clocks start.
Day 90 onwardPlan for TDI ending at 26 weeks. Track the two-year lawsuit deadline. Get a rough net settlement estimate from your lawyer.Request mediation within 60 days of service if a case is filed. Keep every court date; mediation does not pause the case.

What will a settlement really leave for the house?

Gross settlement figures mislead. In a New Jersey injury case, the lawyer's contingent fee is capped by court rule and calculated on the net recovery after case costs, while liens for medical care are not deducted before the fee. The caps under R. 1:21-7(c) and (d) are:

Maximum contingent fees in NJ tort cases, R. 1:21-7(c)
Portion of the net recoveryMaximum fee
First $750,00033⅓%
Next $750,00030%
Next $750,00025%
Next $750,00020%
Above $3,000,000Reasonable fee set on application to the court
Client who was a minor or incapacitated, settled before a jury is sworn25%

Then subtract liens: a health plan, Medicare, Medicaid or a provider that paid crash-related bills may have a claim on the recovery. Your lawyer can tell you which liens apply and whether they can be reduced. What is left is the household number, and that is the number to put in front of a servicer or mediator.

Net-to-household worksheet

Illustration only. Your fee agreement may be lower than the cap, and only your lawyer can confirm liens.

With these example numbers: net recovery $57,500, maximum fee $19,167, after liens $32,333, after catching up the mortgage $18,333.

If the figure at the bottom is small or negative, that is not a reason to give up on the claim. It is a reason to lean harder on PIP, TDI and servicer relief now, and to talk to a lawyer about whether the other driver's coverage, or your own underinsured motorist coverage, is big enough. In our intake data, 42% of callers did not know whether they had UM coverage at all.

Behind on the mortgage because of someone else's driving?

A short New Jersey questionnaire checks whether a lawyer's office may review your injury claim, including lost wages, for free.

Start the NJ accident questionnaire Advertisement. A sponsoring law firm may contact you. It does not handle foreclosure cases and is not the court mediation program.

Questions people ask

Can my lender foreclose while my injury case is still pending?

Yes. The injury claim and the mortgage are separate. A pending claim does not stop a foreclosure; the protections that matter are the 120-day federal waiting period, the Notice of Intention, your right to cure up to final judgment and the mediation program.

How much does PIP pay for lost wages in NJ?

The standard benefit is up to $100 a week, with a $5,200 total per accident, and never more than your normal net income (N.J.S.A. 39:6A-4(b)). You get nothing if you declined the Extra PIP Package, and more if you bought higher income continuation. NJ TDI you can collect is deducted.

Can I get NJ Temporary Disability and PIP at the same time?

You can receive both, but TDI is deducted from PIP income continuation, so PIP only fills the gap up to your limit. TDI pays 85% of your average weekly wage up to $1,119 a week in 2026, for up to 26 weeks.

Is the NJ Foreclosure Mediation Program free?

Yes. State law says the homeowner pays no fees to take part, and the required housing counseling is free through the program. You must ask within 60 days of being served, or later by motion before the sale.

Does foreclosure mediation stop the sheriff sale?

Not by itself. Mediation does not stay the case unless a judge orders it, so keep filing what the court requires. A complete loss mitigation application sent to the servicer more than 37 days before a sale does bar the servicer from holding the sale while it is being decided.

Can I catch up after the foreclosure is filed?

Yes, up to final judgment, by paying the missed payments, late charges and capped court costs and attorney fees (N.J.S.A. 2A:50-57). You can use this right once every 18 months.
